title: Batch, streaming and time
summary: Batch and streaming are points on one latency spectrum; handling event time, late data and duplicates correctly matters more than the choice of engine.

blocks.text: 6.1 A spectrum, not a binary

Batch processing runs a job over a bounded set of data, such as yesterday's orders. Stream processing runs continuously over an unbounded sequence of events. In between, **micro-batch** runs small batch jobs very frequently. All three can compute the same results; they differ in latency, cost and how hard correctness is to get right.

head: Mode
Typical latency
Examples
Main difficulty
rows: Spark Structured Streaming, scheduled incremental loads every few minutes
Small files, overlapping runs, state between batches

blocks.text: A useful way to think about it: **batch is streaming over bounded data**. The concepts in this chapter apply to batch too; batch hides them by waiting until most data has arrived.

Choose the slowest mode that meets the requirement. Each step towards real time multiplies operational cost: always-on infrastructure, state to manage, on-call for a system that never stops. See chapter 19 for micro-batching and chapter 20 for stream processing.
6.2 Event time and processing time

Every event has at least two timestamps. **Event time** is when it happened in the real world: the moment a user tapped *buy*. **Processing time** is when the system handles it. The gap between them, called **skew** or **lag**, varies: network delays, a phone offline in a tunnel for an hour, a partner uploading yesterday's file, a pipeline restarting after an outage.

blocks.title: Events arriving out of order
blocks.text:
event        e1      e2      e3      e4      e5
event time   10:00   10:01   10:02   10:03   10:04
arrived at   10:00   10:01   10:02   10:09   10:04

arrival order: e1, e2, e3, e5, e4   (e4 is 6 minutes late)

Business questions are almost always about event time: *how many orders were placed between 10:00 and 11:00?* Grouping by processing time is easier, because the engine only looks at its own clock, but it produces wrong answers whenever data arrives late and different answers every time data is replayed. A third timestamp, **ingestion time** (when the platform received the event), is useful for incremental loading and debugging but is not a substitute for event time.

Partitioning a lake table by ingestion date and letting analysts filter on it as if it were the business date is a common source of off-by-one-day errors. Keep both columns and be explicit about which one each table is partitioned on.
6.3 Windows and watermarks

Aggregations over unbounded streams are computed per **window**. **Tumbling** windows are fixed and non-overlapping (every 5 minutes). **Sliding** or hopping windows overlap (10-minute windows every minute). **Session** windows close after a gap of inactivity per key, which suits user sessions.

A streaming engine must decide when a window is complete enough to emit and to drop its state. It cannot wait forever, so it tracks a **watermark**: an estimate that *no more events with event time earlier than W are expected*. A common heuristic is the maximum event time seen minus a tolerated delay. When the watermark passes the end of a window, the engine finalizes it.

blocks.title: Spark Structured Streaming: 5-minute windows with a 10-minute watermark
blocks.text:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

clicks = (spark.readStream
          .format("kafka")
          .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", "broker:9092")
          .option("subscribe", "clicks")
          .load())

parsed = clicks.select(
    F.from_json(F.col("value").cast("string"),
                "page STRING, event_time TIMESTAMP").alias("e")
).select("e.*")

counts = (parsed
          .withWatermark("event_time", "10 minutes")
          .groupBy(F.window("event_time", "5 minutes"), "page")
          .count())

The watermark delay is a trade-off between **completeness** and **latency**. A short delay emits results quickly but treats more events as late. A long delay captures more events but holds results and state longer, which costs memory.
6.4 Late data
Data arriving after the watermark has passed its window is **late**. There are only a few options, and the right one depends on the consumer.

items: **Drop it**: simplest; acceptable for monitoring metrics where approximate counts are fine. Count what was dropped.
**Allowed lateness**: keep window state a while longer and emit an updated result when late events arrive (Flink supports this directly). Consumers must accept updates.
**Side output**: route late events to a separate stream or table for later reconciliation.

**Batch correction**: let streaming produce fast provisional numbers and a later batch job recompute final numbers from the complete data. This is the core idea behind the Lambda architecture (chapter 39).

blocks.title: Mobile app revenue
blocks.text: A mobile game records purchases on the device and uploads them when online. About 97% arrive within a minute, 2.5% within a day, and a few within a week.
items: A streaming job with a 2-minute watermark feeds a live operations dashboard labelled as provisional.
A daily batch job recomputes each event date for the last 7 days from the raw event table and overwrites those partitions.
Finance reads only the batch table, closing each day after 7 days.

blocks.text: 6.5 Delivery guarantees

head: Guarantee
Meaning
How it arises
Consequence
rows: Each event is processed zero or one times
Each event is processed one or more times
Process, then commit offsets; retry on failure
Each event affects the result exactly once
At-least-once plus idempotent or transactional sink

blocks.text: Networks and machines fail, so a message can be delivered more than once or its acknowledgement can be lost. True exactly-once *delivery* is not achievable in general. What systems achieve is exactly-once *effect* on state and output: Flink checkpoints its operator state together with source offsets and uses two-phase commit sinks; Kafka offers idempotent producers and transactions so that a read-process-write cycle within Kafka commits atomically. These guarantees end at the system boundary: a non-transactional external sink can still receive duplicates.

A vendor claim of exactly-once usually covers one engine and specific sources and sinks. Ask: exactly-once from where to where, under which failure modes? Check the current documentation for the connectors you actually use.
6.6 Idempotency in practice

An operation is **idempotent** if running it twice gives the same result as running it once. Idempotent writes turn at-least-once delivery into exactly-once results, and they also make retries and backfills safe. It is the single most valuable property of a data pipeline.

items: **Upsert on a key**: `MERGE` on a primary or event id; replays update the same rows instead of adding new ones.
**Deterministic partition overwrite**: a job for date D replaces exactly the partition for D; rerunning produces the same partition.
**Deduplicate on an event id**: producers assign a unique id at creation; consumers drop ids already seen.
**Avoid non-determinism**: `now()`, random ids or unordered `LIMIT` inside transformations make reruns differ. Pass the logical run date as a parameter.

blocks.title: Idempotent upsert (Snowflake, also valid in Spark SQL on Iceberg)
blocks.text:
MERGE INTO silver.orders AS t
USING staging.orders_batch AS s
  ON t.order_id = s.order_id
WHEN MATCHED AND s.updated_at > t.updated_at THEN UPDATE SET
  status     = s.status,
  amount     = s.amount,
  updated_at = s.updated_at
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (order_id, status, amount, updated_at)
  VALUES (s.order_id, s.status, s.amount, s.updated_at);

Note that the source batch must itself contain at most one row per `order_id`; otherwise `MERGE` fails or behaves nondeterministically. Deduplicate the batch first, keeping the latest version per key.

blocks.title: Design a payments counter
blocks.text: A payments service publishes events to Kafka with at-least-once delivery. Finance wants hourly totals per merchant, visible within 5 minutes and correct to the cent by the next morning. About 0.1% of events arrive up to 6 hours late. Choose processing modes, watermark settings, how late events are handled, and how duplicates are removed. Say which table finance reads and why.
hints: Does each event carry a unique id and an event timestamp?
Separate provisional numbers from final numbers.

items: Batch, micro-batch and streaming form a latency spectrum; pick the slowest that meets the need.
Business questions use event time; processing time is easier but wrong for late or replayed data.
Watermarks estimate completeness and trade latency against completeness.
Late data can be dropped, updated, side-output or corrected by a later batch.
Exactly-once is an effect, achieved with at-least-once delivery plus idempotent or transactional sinks.

blocks.q: What does a watermark of 10:05 tell a streaming engine?
options: It expects no more events with event time earlier than 10:05
All events up to 10:05 processing time have been written to disk
blocks.explain: A watermark is a completeness estimate in event time. Events older than it are late; they are not necessarily dropped (that depends on configuration), and it says nothing about processing time checkpoints.

blocks.q: A job commits Kafka offsets only after writing results, and the sink is an append-only table. What happens after a crash between writing and committing?
options: The same events are written twice
blocks.explain: This is at-least-once: on restart the job reprocesses from the last committed offset and appends the same results again. An idempotent or transactional sink would prevent the duplicates.

blocks.q: Which change makes a daily job safe to rerun?
options: Append results and add a `loaded_at = now()` column
Run it twice and keep the larger result
Overwrite exactly the partition for the logical run date, computed only from inputs for that date
Use processing time for all filters
blocks.explain: A deterministic partition overwrite is idempotent. Appending with `now()` creates duplicates that differ only by timestamp, and processing-time filters change with each run.

blocks.q: Why is grouping streaming revenue by processing time risky?
options: It is always slower than event time
Processing time is not available in Kafka
Late and replayed events are counted in the wrong period and results change on replay
blocks.explain: Processing time reflects when the system saw the event, not when it happened. A backlog after an outage would land in the wrong hour, and a replay would produce different numbers.
